pharm: Fluoroquinolone; inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase & topoisomerase IV
quick: 400 mg loading day 1, then 200 mg once daily
summary: Sparfloxacin is a long-acting di-fluoroquinolone antibacterial used for community-acquired pneumonia and acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis. It is NOT FDA-approved and has been withdrawn or never marketed in many countries because of marked QT-interval prolongation and severe phototoxicity. It is contraindicated with other QT-prolonging drugs, and patients must avoid sun/UV exposure during therapy and for at least 5 days afterwards. Like all fluoroquinolones it carries a risk of tendinitis, tendon rupture and CNS effects.
indications: Acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis

dosage.d: 400 mg as a single loading dose on day 1, then 200 mg once daily
dosage.t: Total course 10 days (loading day + 9 days of 200 mg)
dosage.n: Long half-life allows once-daily maintenance dosing

dosage.d: 400 mg loading dose on day 1, then 200 mg once daily
400 mg loading dose on day 1, then 200 mg every 48 hours
dosage.n: Reduce maintenance frequency in significant renal impairment

admin: Take once daily at about the same time each day
May be taken with or without food
Separate from antacids, sucralfate, iron, zinc and other multivalent cations by at least 4 hours (give cations 4 hours after the dose) to avoid chelation
Avoid sunlight, sunlamps and UV exposure during therapy and for at least 5 days after the last dose
Maintain adequate hydration; complete the full prescribed course
moa: Bactericidal fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for bacterial DNA replication, transcription, repair and recombination, leading to cell death.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to sparfloxacin or other quinolones
Known QT-interval prolongation or congenital long-QT syndrome
Concomitant class IA (e.g. quinidine, procainamide) or class III (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol) antiarrhythmics or other QT-prolonging drugs
relative: History of tendon disorders or prior fluoroquinolone-associated reaction
Seizure disorder or other CNS conditions lowering seizure threshold
monitor: ECG/QT interval, especially in at-risk patients
Tendon pain/swelling — stop immediately if suspected

preg: Not recommended in pregnancy; fluoroquinolones are generally avoided due to potential effects on developing cartilage. Use only if no safer alternative and benefit outweighs risk.
lact: Fluoroquinolones are excreted in breast milk; avoid during breastfeeding or discontinue nursing, given potential effects on infant cartilage and risk of photosensitization.
renal: Reduce maintenance dosing in renal impairment — give the 200 mg maintenance dose every 48 hours when CrCl <50 mL/min. Loading dose unchanged.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; limited specific data. Discontinue if signs of hepatotoxicity develop.

major: Class IA (quinidine, procainamide) and class III (amiodarone, sotalol) antiarrhythmics — additive QT prolongation/torsades (contraindicated)
Other QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, antipsychotics, tricyclic antidepressants, cisapride, methadone) — additive torsades risk (contraindicated/avoid)
Drugs causing hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia (loop/thiazide diuretics) — heighten QT/torsades risk
moderate: Multivalent cations (antacids, sucralfate, iron, zinc, magnesium/aluminium) — reduced sparfloxacin absorption; separate by 4 hours
NSAIDs — may increase CNS stimulation/seizure risk
Drugs that cause photosensitivity — additive phototoxicity
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; may add to CNS effects.
interactions.diagnostics: Fluoroquinolones may produce false-positive urine opiate immunoassay results (class effect).

emergency: Palpitations, syncope or sudden collapse (possible torsades de pointes) — seek emergency care
Anaphylaxis or severe skin reaction (may occur after first dose)
Tendon pain/snap/swelling — stop drug, rest limb, seek care
New seizures, severe confusion or hallucinations
Severe blistering sunburn-like skin reaction after light exposure

monitoring: ECG/QT interval, particularly with cardiac risk factors or other QT-prolonging therapy
Serum potassium and magnesium; correct before and during therapy
Signs of tendinitis/tendon rupture (especially >60 yrs, on steroids)
Skin for phototoxicity throughout treatment and 5 days after
counsel: Avoid sunlight, sunlamps and UV light during treatment and for at least 5 days after your last dose — even brief exposure can cause severe skin reactions
Wear protective clothing and use sunscreen if exposure is unavoidable
Tell your doctor about any heart-rhythm problems or medicines for heart rhythm — this drug can affect the heart's QT interval
Seek urgent help for palpitations, fainting or severe dizziness
Stop and call your doctor at the first sign of tendon pain, swelling or a snap
Take iron, antacids or indigestion remedies at least 4 hours after this medicine
Avoid alcohol and complete the full course
pk: Well absorbed orally; therapeutic levels within hours
Once-daily dosing supported by long half-life
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light, per labeling
pearls: Pending clinical review - not FDA-approved (openFDA returned no matches); withdrawn or never marketed in many countries
Marked QT prolongation — contraindicated with class IA and class III antiarrhythmics and other QT-prolonging drugs; correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia first
Severe phototoxicity is the hallmark adverse effect — strict sun/UV avoidance during therapy and for at least 5 days afterwards
Long half-life (~16-20 h) allows once-daily maintenance dosing after a day-1 loading dose
Class fluoroquinolone risks apply: tendinitis/tendon rupture, CNS effects, peripheral neuropathy
Separate from antacids, iron, zinc and other multivalent cations by at least 4 hours
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue the once-daily schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Discontinue the drug; obtain ECG and monitor cardiac rhythm closely for QT prolongation/torsades de pointes. Correct electrolytes (potassium, magnesium). Provide supportive care, maintain hydration and observe for CNS effects/seizures. No specific antidote; not efficiently removed by dialysis.
